claim: Most MTD tests run in simulation
quote: more work needs to be done in rethinking approaches to testing it in realistic ways, simulating how actual attackers might approach breaching the network.
issue: Jalowski never says most MTD tests run in simulation; the clause is carried by co-cited cho2020 (Sec. VIII-B). Recorded only so the bracket is not read as Jalowski supporting it.

claim: Most tests run against attacker models far simpler than an APT
quote: Effective models must account for attacker capabilities, realistic attack vectors, and adaptive strategies, moving beyond the simplistic assumptions that currently dominate the literature.
locator: Sec. 6, p. 9 printed (PDF p. 9); with Sec. 4.3, p. 8: 'testing against active scanning (Nmap [ 52]) is too naive. Advanced Persistent Threats (APTs) ... utilize Passive Reconnaissance'
issue: 'dominate' carries 'most', and Sec. 4.3 sets the simplistic models against APTs. 'far' is an intensifier the source's 'too simplistic' roughly bears.

claim: Jalowski et al. call the attacker model 'the most glaring flaw in the MTD literature' (p. 8)
quote: The most glaring flaw in the MTD literature is the ill-defined attacker models [ 7], which are often too simplistic or based on completely unrealistic assumptions.
locator: Sec. 4.3, p. 8 printed (PDF p. 8); pinpoint correct
issue: Quote is verbatim and the pinpoint right, but the flaw Jalowski names is 'the ill-defined attacker models', not 'the attacker model'; dropping 'ill-defined' shifts the flaw from how models are defined to the attacker model as such. The sentence also cites the authors' own 2022 survey [7], so it restates an earlier finding.
fix_text: 'call the attacker model' -> 'call ill-defined attacker models'

claim: MTD is typically tested against active scanning, such as Nmap
quote: To make matters worse, it is commonly calculated using simple Nmap scans [52] as a baseline
locator: Sec. 5, p. 9 printed (PDF p. 9); with Sec. 4.3, p. 8: 'testing against active scanning (Nmap [ 52]) is too naive'
issue: 'commonly' is said of ASP's baseline; Sec. 4.3 says testing against active scanning is too naive without saying it is typical. Together they carry 'typically'.

claim: An APT attacker uses passive reconnaissance to stay hidden
quote: Advanced Persistent Threats (APTs) [ 53,54] utilize Passive Reconnaissance [ 55] to remain in the shadows and learn mutation patterns over time.
issue: Jalowski itself cites [53-55] (Alshamrani; Chen; a passive-reconnaissance source) for this, so it is a survey's restatement; acceptable for a survey-finding sentence.

claim: MTD mechanisms cannot be compared across evaluations because each evaluation chooses its own metrics
quote: While these individual approaches are not necessarily incorrect, the lack of a universal metric prevents any objective cross-technique comparison
locator: Sec. 3.1, p. 5 printed (PDF p. 5); also Sec. 1: 'many authors propose their own idea on how to test the effectiveness of MTD strategies, using their own metrics and frameworks' (p. 2)

claim: Jalowski's finding is that MTD attacker models in general lack the properties of an APT attacker
quote: The most glaring flaw in the MTD literature is the ill-defined attacker models [ 7], which are often too simplistic or based on completely unrealistic assumptions.
locator: Sec. 4.3, p. 8 printed (PDF p. 8); Sec. 6, p. 9
issue: Jalowski finds attacker models 'often' too simplistic and names specific missing traits (passive reconnaissance, learning mutation patterns, understanding the scheme); it does not find that they lack the properties of an APT attacker in general. Hedge 'often' dropped, scope widened to 'the properties'.
fix_text: 'lack the properties of an APT attacker' -> 'lack several properties of an APT attacker'
